category_section_description: Practice one concept family at a time with focused equation and code-reading questions.

assessment_phases.label: Pre-test
assessment_phases.description: Check your starting understanding before practice.

assessment_phases.label: Post-test
assessment_phases.description: Measure progress after completing at least one successful lesson run.

category_quizzes.label: Bellman Equations
category_quizzes.description: Policy evaluation, Bellman expectation, Bellman optimality, and terminal backups.

category_quizzes.label: Policy Improvement
category_quizzes.description: Greedy improvement, value iteration, and action-value comparisons.

category_quizzes.label: Monte Carlo Returns
category_quizzes.description: First-visit returns, complete episodes, and sample-average updates.

category_quizzes.label: TD Control
category_quizzes.description: TD targets, Q-learning, SARSA, terminal guards, and bootstrapping.

category_quizzes.label: Exploration Schedules
category_quizzes.description: Epsilon-greedy behavior, decay, and exploration/exploitation tradeoffs.

questions.prompt: What does policy evaluation repeatedly update for each state?
options: The expected return under the current policy
The number of available actions
The exploration rate schedule
The animation playback speed

questions.prompt: Which operation makes value iteration different from policy evaluation?
options: Taking the maximum over action values
Averaging rewards across every episode
Sampling only the first state in an episode
Replacing gamma with alpha

questions.prompt: What does policy improvement do after state values have been estimated?
options: It chooses the greedy action for each state using the current value table
It averages returns over complete episodes
It replaces the value table with transition probabilities
It resets every Q-value to zero before the next episode

questions.prompt: What does a transition probability describe in FrozenLake?
options: How likely the environment is to move to a next state after an action
How many times a state has been visited
The reward assigned to every terminal state
The number of frames rendered per episode

questions.prompt: How is a terminal state typically handled in value updates?
options: Its future value contribution is treated as zero
Its reward is ignored completely
Its transition probabilities are set equal to epsilon
Its action space doubles in size

questions.prompt: Which expression matches a one-step Bellman expectation backup for V_pi(s)?
options: Sum over actions and next states of pi(a|s) P(s'|s,a) [r + gamma V(s')]
Max over actions of alpha times the previous Q-value
Average all rewards in the replay buffer without discounting
Reward minus gamma times the previous state value

questions.prompt: What changes when moving from the Bellman expectation equation to the Bellman optimality equation?
options: The policy-weighted action average becomes a max over actions
The discount factor is removed
Transition probabilities are ignored
Terminal rewards are always set to zero

questions.prompt:
Read the policy-evaluation backup:

value += action_prob * transition_prob * (reward + gamma * V[next_state])

What does multiplying by both probabilities do?
options: It weights each successor contribution by how likely the policy and environment make it
It forces the update to choose the greedy action
It prevents terminal states from contributing rewards
It converts V into a Q-table

questions.prompt: In a Bellman backup, why should a terminal successor contribute no discounted future value?
options: There are no future decisions after termination, so only the immediate reward remains
Terminal states always have negative rewards
The transition probability is always zero
The learning rate becomes one at terminal states

questions.prompt: Which sequence describes policy iteration?
options: Evaluate the current policy, then improve it greedily from the value estimates
Choose random actions forever, then average final rewards
Update Q with the sampled next action, then lower epsilon
Render an episode, then copy its frames into the next policy

questions.prompt:
A policy-improvement loop computes action_values for a state and then runs:

best_action = max(range(action_count), key=lambda action: action_values[action])

What policy does this produce for that state?
options: A greedy policy that chooses the action with the largest backed-up value
A uniformly random policy over all actions
A first-visit Monte Carlo policy
A policy that always chooses the action with the lowest reward

questions.prompt: Why does value iteration repeatedly sweep over states?
options: Value information has to propagate backward through successor-state backups
Every state must be visited exactly once and then frozen
The transition model changes after every sweep
The discount factor increases after each state

questions.prompt:
In value iteration, this line appears inside a state update:

new_values[state] = max(action_values)

What does this line represent?
options: The Bellman optimality backup selecting the best action value
The policy expectation over all action probabilities
A Monte Carlo average over full episode returns
The epsilon-greedy behavior action

questions.prompt: When does first-visit Monte Carlo prediction update a state's value?
options: After the episode is complete and the first-visit return is known
Immediately after every action
Only when the agent reaches the start state again
Before the environment is reset

questions.prompt: Why does first-visit Monte Carlo ignore repeated visits to the same state in one episode?
options: It only keeps the return from the first occurrence of that state
It assumes repeated states are impossible
It wants to maximize the exploration rate
It replaces returns with transition probabilities

questions.prompt: What is the return G_t in Monte Carlo prediction?
options: The discounted sum of rewards from time t to the end of the episode
The immediate reward only
The maximum Q-value in the next state
The probability of selecting the greedy action

questions.prompt: Why is first-visit Monte Carlo not a bootstrapping method?
options: It waits for complete returns instead of using a current value estimate in the target
It updates before any reward is observed
It always uses max_a Q(s,a)
It requires a transition probability table

questions.prompt:
Read this return calculation:

G = 0.0
discount = 1.0
for _, _, reward in episode[index:]:
    G += discount * reward
    discount *= gamma

What does discount *= gamma do?
options: It makes later rewards count by progressively higher powers of gamma
It increases the learning rate after every reward
It makes every reward count equally
It selects the next action from the policy

questions.prompt: After appending a new first-visit return for a state, why is V[state] set to the mean of returns[state]?
options: The value estimate is the sample average of observed returns from that state
The largest observed return is always unbiased
The latest reward replaces all prior evidence
The state transition probability must sum to one

questions.prompt: What is the TD target used by Q-learning?
options: Reward plus discounted best next-state action value
Reward plus the current state's maximum value
Average episode reward minus epsilon
Discount factor times the previous action probability

questions.prompt: Why is Q-learning considered off-policy?
options: It learns from the greedy target even when behavior includes exploration
It requires complete episodes before every update
It evaluates only a fixed stochastic policy
It cannot be used with discrete state spaces

questions.prompt: Why is SARSA considered on-policy?
options: Its TD target uses the next action that the behavior policy actually sampled
It waits for the end of the episode before every update
It computes a maximum over all next-state actions
It ignores the discount factor during bootstrapping

questions.prompt: Which target is used by one-step TD prediction for V(s)?
options: r + gamma V(s')
max_a pi(a|s)
The average of every return in the episode
epsilon / action_count

questions.prompt: What is the TD error in the update V(s) <- V(s) + alpha [target - V(s)]?
options: target - V(s)
V(s) - reward
alpha * gamma
epsilon + reward

questions.prompt:
Read this Q-learning target:

best_next = max(Q[next_state])
td_target = reward + gamma * best_next

Why does it use max(Q[next_state])?
options: Q-learning learns the greedy target policy even if behavior was exploratory
SARSA requires the largest next action
Monte Carlo methods need a next-state bootstrap
It averages over the behavior policy

questions.prompt:
Read this SARSA target:

bootstrap = 0.0 if next_action is None else Q[next_state][next_action]
td_target = reward + gamma * bootstrap

Why is next_action used instead of max(Q[next_state])?
options: SARSA is on-policy and backs up the action actually sampled by the behavior policy
SARSA ignores the behavior policy
SARSA cannot handle terminal states
SARSA is a complete-episode Monte Carlo method

questions.prompt: A TD update sets bootstrap = 0.0 when terminated is true. What bug does this prevent?
options: Adding discounted future value after the episode has already ended
Using too small a learning rate
Choosing greedy actions too often
Recording a reward in the trace

questions.prompt: What does the discount factor gamma primarily control?
options: How much future rewards influence the current estimate
How many episodes are stored in memory
How often the policy is rendered
How many actions the environment exposes

questions.prompt: What does a state-value function estimate?
options: The expected long-term return from a state
The immediate reward of the previous action only
The probability that the episode will never end
The number of code lines executed in the update step

questions.prompt: What is the role of epsilon in epsilon-greedy action selection?
options: It controls how often the agent explores instead of exploiting
It controls the Bellman residual threshold
It scales the animation frame size
It replaces the reward function

questions.prompt: With epsilon-greedy action selection, what happens as epsilon decreases?
options: The agent chooses random exploratory actions less often
The discount factor increases
The TD target becomes a Monte Carlo return
The reward function becomes deterministic
The random action sampled when random.random() < epsilon
The argmax action after the if statement
Both branches are always greedy
Neither branch changes behavior

questions.prompt: Why do many epsilon schedules keep a minimum epsilon floor?
options: To preserve some exploration instead of becoming permanently greedy too early
To make gamma larger than one
To force every terminal state to be revisited
To convert Q-learning into policy evaluation
